scope: Twenty-seventh expansion batch, first mixed-context selection set:12 exercises in four read/write/use/speak triplets. Four established routine changes, four maintained personal practices and four current evidence-based judgments share one three-way relationship. The whole construction ending is missing. One identical five-pattern instruction is used for every item, without identifying the answer's function or supplying a naru/suru ending. This is bounded, less-scaffolded selection, not unrestricted cloze or all-family mixed coverage.

sources.publisher: The Japan Foundation, Minna no Kyozai
sources.section: Actual HTML heading Ｖようになります, structure and explanations A/B. Dictionary verbs describe changed habits; potential verbs describe changes in ability/circumstances. This set uses dictionary verbs for routines, not a potential-only rule. Examples include deliberate study and changed external conditions. Do not universalize the elementary teacher note's restrictions on negative attachment or change verbs, old JLPT labels, or the dated space-travel prediction.

authoringNotes: All12 scenarios are original and need independent linguistic review, including all36 literal accepted endings. The same three-way relationship and same five-pattern pool are used throughout. Four routine changes accept you-ni-natta/natteiru, four practices accept you-ni-shiteiru/koto-ni-shiteiru plus habitual you-ni-suru, and four current judgments accept hazu-da/you-da and de-aru variants. Accepted alternatives are not wrong buttons.

Compared with the earlier supplied-pattern exercises, this set blanks the complete ending and mixes three functions. It does not tell each question which function, conjugation or ending to choose. The full English translation remains visible and defines the intended message; factual compatibility alone is not the task. Do not infer that a story's only grammatical description is its model answer.

The common instruction asks for one listed pattern in a complete, uncontracted plain form, written in hiragana without extra particles or auxiliary constructions. Thus te-ru contractions, kanji spellings, omitted copulas, desu/masu, sentence-final particles, explanatory no-da and aspectual te-kuru combinations are outside this explicit practice format, not bad Japanese. Plain de-aru is accepted without recommending it as equally conversational.

The change cases include a naturally acquired reading habit, a deliberately cultivated diary habit and externally changed software/language use. They do not equate naru with lack of human intention, or ordinary dictionary verbs with newly acquired ability. Current-result natteiru and completed-change natta are fitting ways to report the same established change in these contexts.

The practice cases explicitly give existing personal rules and continuing care, with lapses. Their current maintenance is distinct from merely announcing or retelling the original decision. The shared koto-ni-shiteiru alternative frames a personal rule rather than pretending you-ni-suru and koto-ni-suru are identical in all uses. The recurring meeting-morning, idea-recording, shopping and answering frames also permit plain nonpast you-ni-suru as a generic account of repeated care; you-ni-shiteiru foregrounds the maintained state more explicitly. This sentence-specific judgment comes from editorial review, not an equivalence stated in the Minna lesson, which teaches you-ni-shiteimasu for habitual care. It is not a rule that every nonpast you-ni-suru describes an existing habit.

The inference cases have observations but no direct verification of an entire routine, an earlier baseline, or the person's private intention. Newspaper markings, posting records, filled bags and recordings support current judgments. Publication timestamps are not guaranteed writing timestamps; repeated samples do not prove every occurrence. Keep stronger reasoned expectation versus evidential impression as a nuance, not a confidence-number test.

The article inventory and previous change/effort, action, intent and degree records were screened. Koto-ni-naru could give an arrangement account of workplace changes; tsumori, rashii, so-da, wake-da and other paraphrases can fit other intended messages. They are not in this common five-pattern pool. The set does not claim every grammar family has now received mixed-context selection.

All five institutional source pages were read directly. Initial JPF extraction split ruby and headings, missing the change title and beginning too late in the effort lesson; ruby-aware HTML extraction recovered the complete charts, examples and teacher notes. A guessed Bunpro koto-ni-shiteiru URL returned404 and is not evidence. Its actual koto-ni-suru lesson was inspected as corroboration but was not needed as a primary citation.

All341 earlier records and identities remain unchanged. Add one mixed-selection article section, its reference bullet, source record, README/contract scope and focused regressions. The earlier supplied-pattern coverage statements remain accurate for those earlier files. No Android, counter, schema, grading or SRS changes; broader mixed selection remains open.
